newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium's Cockerill rules out mergers.
newsitem.headline: Belgium's Cockerill rules out mergers.

text.p: Belgium's largest steel-maker Cockerill Sambre, which has been studying ways to safeguard the future of steel in Belgium's industrial Walloon region, on Wednesday ruled out any mergers with two smaller steel makers.
In a joint statement with privately-held Usines Gustave Boel (UGB), the two companies said they were not complementary and there could no worthwhile economic synergies between the two.

"An examination of profitability, sensitivity to the economic environment and the financial needs have led to the conclusion that a lasting future for Boel could not be guaranteed without weakening Cockerill," the statement said.
Cockerill shares which were suspended on the Brussels bourse ahead of the Cockerill-Boel announcement ended the day one franc lower at 129 after peaking at 131.
Boel is meanwhile still in talks with Dutch steel maker Hoogovens over a 50-50 joint venture, which it hopes will be finalised by the end of the year.
Banque Bruxelles Lambert analyst Olivier Heuschling said a Boel-Hoogovens venture would give Hoogovens increased access to the French market, a market where Cockerill was very prominent.

The Walloon regional government has encouraged contact between the region's steel firms, which are struggling like others in a sector weighed down by overcapacity, cheap imports from the east and steel's heavily cyclical nature.
Through its steel investment arm, the region is a majority shareholder in both Cockerill, which produced 6.3 million tonnes of steel in 1995, and in smaller loss-making Forges de Clabecq.
But Cockerill, which produces flat-steel, also ruled out any possibilities of merging with Clabecq.

"Cockerill doesn't produce the same product as Clabecq, there is no common product between the two and we don't see any advantages of merging," said Cockerill chief executive officer Philippe Delaunois. "There will never be any merger with Clabecq."
Clabecq is the subject of a 1.5 billion Belgian franc ($46.7 million) state aid plan by the Walloon region which is being investigated by the European Commission on competition grounds.
The capital injection was granted by the region to tide the company over until a long term solution could be found.
Analysts question whether Cockerill will be able to avoid taking on Clabecq if that is ultimately what the Walloon government demands.
"This is not only an economic issue, it's political. Normally the majority shareholder has the last say, but Cockerill has always run its own strategy," one said.

Clabecq's chief executive officer Libert Froidmont earlier this month said it saw closer links between steel firms in Belgium's francophone southern region as a way to ensure its survival and the preservation of jobs in the area.
Analysts say a merger with Clabecq would be a drain on Cockerill which slipped into loss in the first half of 1996 after a 1995 full year group net profit of 3.2 billion francs.

"Cockerill Sambre needs a critical mass to survive in the long term in the European Union Steel market, but Clabecq wouldn't give that. It's productivity is poor and it is not cost effecient," BBL's Heuschling said. ($1=32.14 Belgian Franc)
